solution:
First convert the interior angle to degrees: \(\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)^{c} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\times\dfrac{180}{\pi} = 135^\circ\).

At each vertex the interior and exterior angles are supplementary, so each exterior angle \(= 180^\circ - 135^\circ = 45^\circ\).

For a regular polygon of \(n\) sides the exterior angles sum to \(360^\circ\), so \(n = \dfrac{360^\circ}{45^\circ} = 8\).

The polygon has 8 sides.

Let \(A\) and \(B\) be the centres, \(r = 7\) cm, \(AB = 7\sqrt{2}\) cm, and let \(P\), \(P'\) be the points of intersection.

In \(\Delta APB\): \(AP = BP = 7\) and \(AP^2 + BP^2 = 49 + 49 = 98 = (7\sqrt{2})^2 = AB^2\), so \(\angle APB = 90^\circ\) and the triangle is right isosceles. Hence \(\angle PAB = 45^\circ\), and by symmetry the common chord \(PP'\) subtends \(\angle PAP' = 2\times 45^\circ = 90^\circ = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)^{c}\) at each centre.

The common region is made of two equal circular segments, one from each circle, each cut off by the chord \(PP'\) with \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\):
\(\text{segment} = \dfrac{1}{2}r^{2}\theta - \dfrac{1}{2}r^{2}\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}r^{2}(\theta - \sin\theta)\).

\(\therefore\) common area \(= 2\times\dfrac{1}{2}r^{2}(\theta - \sin\theta) = r^{2}(\theta - \sin\theta) = 49\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \sin 90^\circ\right)\).

The area common to both circles is \(49\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 1\right)\) sq.cm.

solution:
Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(QR\); it is the centre of the circle, with radius \(r = \dfrac{18}{2} = 9\) cm. Let the circle cut side \(PQ\) at \(S\) and side \(PR\) at \(T\); the required arc is arc \(ST\) (the part of the circle lying inside the triangle).

In \(\Delta QMS\): \(MQ = MS = 9\) (radii), so it is isosceles, and \(\angle MQS = \angle PQR = 60^\circ\). Hence \(\angle MSQ = 60^\circ\) and \(\angle QMS = 60^\circ\). Similarly \(\angle RMT = 60^\circ\).

Since \(Q\), \(M\), \(R\) are collinear, \(\angle SMT = 180^\circ - 60^\circ - 60^\circ = 60^\circ = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)^{c}\).

\(\therefore\) arc \(ST = r\theta = 9\times\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 3\pi\).

The length of the arc lying within the triangle is \(3\pi\) cm.
diagramNote: Equilateral \Delta PQR of side 18 cm with the circle on QR as diameter (centre M, the midpoint of QR); mark S on PQ and T on PR where the circle cuts the sides, and highlight arc ST inside the triangle with \angle SMT = 60^\circ.

solution:
The angle must be in radians: \(\theta = 60^\circ = 60\times\dfrac{\pi}{180} = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)^{c}\).

From \(s = r\theta\), \(r = \dfrac{s}{\theta} = \dfrac{37.4}{\pi/3} = \dfrac{37.4\times 3}{\pi} = \dfrac{112.2}{\pi}\).

Taking \(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\): \(r = \dfrac{112.2\times 7}{22} = \dfrac{785.4}{22} = 35.7\).

The radius of the circle is \(35.7\) cm.

The bent wire becomes the arc, so \(s = 10\) cm and \(r = 4\) cm.

From \(s = r\theta\), \(\theta = \dfrac{s}{r} = \dfrac{10}{4} = \left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)^{c}\).

Converting to degrees, \(\theta = \dfrac{5}{2}\times\dfrac{180}{\pi} = \dfrac{450}{\pi}\).

The angle subtended at the centre is \(\left(\dfrac{450}{\pi}\right)^\circ\) (about \(143^\circ 14'\)).

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(13 : 22\), which is the ratio of the two ANGLES \(65 : 110\), not of the radii. For arcs of equal length \(r_1\theta_1 = r_2\theta_2\), so the circle with the smaller angle must be the larger one and the correct ratio is \(22 : 13\). The identical slip appears at Exercise 1.2 Q.5.]

Let \(r_{1}\) be the radius of the circle in which the arc subtends \(\theta_{1} = 65^\circ\) and \(r_{2}\) the radius of the circle in which it subtends \(\theta_{2} = 110^\circ\).

In radians, \(\theta_{1} = 65\times\dfrac{\pi}{180} = \left(\dfrac{13\pi}{36}\right)^{c}\) and \(\theta_{2} = 110\times\dfrac{\pi}{180} = \left(\dfrac{22\pi}{36}\right)^{c}\).

The arcs are of the same length, so \(r_{1}\theta_{1} = r_{2}\theta_{2}\), giving
\(\dfrac{r_{1}}{r_{2}} = \dfrac{\theta_{2}}{\theta_{1}} = \dfrac{22\pi/36}{13\pi/36} = \dfrac{22}{13}\).

(The smaller angle belongs to the larger circle, as expected.)

\(\therefore r_{1} : r_{2} = 22 : 13\).
_note: The book's key prints 13 : 22. For the same arc length \(r_1\theta_1 = r_2\theta_2\), so the radius is inversely proportional to the angle: the circle with the SMALLER angle (65^\circ) must have the LARGER radius. Taking the radii in the order the angles are named in the stem (65^\circ then 110^\circ) the ratio is therefore 22 : 13; the printed 13 : 22 is that ratio written in the reverse order (r_2 : r_1).

solution:
Area of the circle \(= \pi r^{2} = 81\pi\), so \(r^{2} = 81\) and \(r = 9\) cm.

The angle in radians is \(\theta = 300^\circ = 300\times\dfrac{\pi}{180} = \left(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right)^{c}\).

Arc length \(s = r\theta = 9\times\dfrac{5\pi}{3} = 15\pi\) cm.

Area of the sector \(= \dfrac{1}{2}r^{2}\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 81\times\dfrac{5\pi}{3} = \dfrac{135\pi}{2}\) sq.cm.

The arc is \(15\pi\) cm long and the corresponding sector has area \(\dfrac{135\pi}{2}\) sq.cm.

The minute hand completes one full turn, \(360^\circ\), in 60 minutes, so it moves through \(\dfrac{360^\circ}{60} = 6^\circ\) in one minute.

The hour hand completes one full turn, \(360^\circ\), in 12 hours \(= 720\) minutes, so it moves through \(\dfrac{360^\circ}{720} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^\circ\) in one minute.

In one minute the gain of the minute hand over the hour hand is the difference of these two movements:
\(6^\circ - \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^\circ = \left(\dfrac{11}{2}\right)^\circ = 5^\circ + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^\circ = 5^\circ + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times 60\right)' = 5^\circ 30'\).

Hence in one minute the minute hand gains \(5^\circ 30'\) on the hour hand.

Speed \(= 36\) km/hr, so in 30 seconds \(= \dfrac{30}{3600}\) hr \(= \dfrac{1}{120}\) hr the train covers
\(s = 36\times\dfrac{1}{120} = 0.3\) km.

The track is the arc, with \(r = 1\) km. From \(s = r\theta\),
\(\theta = \dfrac{s}{r} = \dfrac{0.3}{1} = (0.3)^{c}\).

In degrees, \(\theta = 0.3\times\dfrac{180}{\pi} = \dfrac{54}{\pi} \approx \dfrac{54}{3.1416} \approx 17.1887^\circ\).

Now \(0.1887\times 60 \approx 11.32'\) and \(0.32\times 60 \approx 20''\), so \(\theta \approx 17^\circ 11' 20''\).

The train turns through about \(17^\circ 11' 20''\), that is \(17^\circ 11'\) to the nearest minute.

Radius \(r = \dfrac{40}{2} = 20\) cm, and the chord \(AB = 20\) cm.

In \(\Delta OAB\), \(OA = OB = AB = 20\) cm, so the triangle is equilateral and the angle subtended at the centre is
\(\theta = 60^\circ = 60\times\dfrac{\pi}{180} = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)^{c}\).

The minor arc corresponds to this angle, so \(s = r\theta = 20\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

The length of the minor arc is \(\dfrac{20\pi}{3}\) cm.

Let the four angles in A.P. be \(a-3d,\ a-d,\ a+d,\ a+3d\) (least to greatest).

The angles of a quadrilateral add up to \(360^\circ\):
\((a-3d)+(a-d)+(a+d)+(a+3d) = 4a = 360^\circ\), so \(a = 90^\circ\).

Given the greatest angle is double the least: \(a+3d = 2(a-3d)\), so \(a + 3d = 2a - 6d\), giving \(9d = a = 90^\circ\) and \(d = 10^\circ\).

The angles are \(60^\circ,\ 80^\circ,\ 100^\circ,\ 120^\circ\). Multiplying each by \(\dfrac{\pi}{180}\):

\(60^\circ = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)^{c},\quad 80^\circ = \left(\dfrac{4\pi}{9}\right)^{c},\quad 100^\circ = \left(\dfrac{5\pi}{9}\right)^{c},\quad 120^\circ = \left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)^{c}\).

The angles of the quadrilateral are \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)^{c},\ \left(\dfrac{4\pi}{9}\right)^{c},\ \left(\dfrac{5\pi}{9}\right)^{c}\) and \(\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)^{c}\).
